sources.title: Annie Jump Cannon (Q230650), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-04): label 'Annie Jump Cannon', description 'American astronomer (1863-1941)', born 1863-12-11, died 1941-04-13, Korean label 애니 점프 캐넌. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Annie Jump Cannon' (Britannica Editors), article body read as served. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: American astronomer who in 1901 simplified existing schemes to the spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K and M with ten numbered steps each, which became the universally adopted temperature sequence; she classified spectra for more than 225,000 stars, published in nine volumes as the Henry Draper Catalogue (1918-24), and discovered about 300 variable stars and 5 novae; assistant at Harvard Observatory from 1896 under Pickering alongside Williamina Fleming and Antonia Maury, curator of astronomical photographs from 1911, the Henry Draper Extension, honours including the first Oxford honorary doctorate to a woman (1925) and the 1931 Henry Draper Medal, and appointment to the Harvard faculty only in 1938. Scholarly modern reference.

Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry 'Cannon, Annie Jump' (as reproduced on Encyclopedia.com), full entry read: her Wellesley and Radcliffe studies, the Harvard staff from 1896, the definitive Harvard system of spectral classification rearranged from the earlier letter groups, the 1901 catalogue of 1,122 stars, the Henry Draper Catalogue of 225,300 stars classified in the interval from 1911 to 1915 and published by 1924, about 47,000 further classifications in the Extension and later zone catalogues, adoption by the International Astronomical Union in 1922, her rate of more than three stars a minute and ability to duplicate her classifications later, her tendency to note peculiarities in the spectrum, Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin's remark that she never published a controversial word or speculative thought, and her honours. Scholarly dictionary; some of its praise (concentration, charm) is retrospective, and its remark linking her deafness to concentration is not used.

Encyclopedia of World Biography, entry 'Annie Jump Cannon' (as reproduced on Encyclopedia.com), read in full: studies at Wellesley and Radcliffe, her Harvard post, 225,300 stars, the 1922 International Astronomical Union adoption and half a year photographing the southern sky at Arequipa in Peru, the observation that honours after 1920 resulted from initiatives of Harlow Shapley and Henry Norris Russell because of the lack of recognition at Harvard itself, the 1931 Draper Medal and the 1932 Ellen Richards Prize which she turned over to the American Astronomical Society to found the Annie Jump Cannon Award, Margaret Rossiter's comment that she wanted more recognition for younger women, and her 1938 non-faculty appointment as William Cranch Bond Astronomer. Reference biography; the counter-voice on institutional recognition.

Science and Its Times, entry 'Annie Jump Cannon' (as reproduced on Encyclopedia.com), read in full: Pickering hired her in 1896, she initially classified 5,000 stars a month and eventually about 300 an hour, Pickering asked her for a better method of recording star information, she outlined ten star categories by 1901, she was the sole classifier so that her observations were consistent, she insisted that even the faintest stars be included and that both hemispheres be photographed, and she compiled more astronomical data than any other individual. Student-oriented reference work; its rate figure differs from the other sources.

MacTutor History of Mathematics archive (University of St Andrews), biography 'Annie Jump Cannon', read in full: her early education and photography, hiring by Pickering in 1896, the Second Catalogue of Variable Stars (1907), her classification rate rising from 1,000 stars in three years to 200 an hour by 1913, Pickering's 1918 preface stating that the Henry Draper classification was begun on 2 October 1911 and practically completed on 30 September 1915 with 242,093 spectra classified, the 1922 adoption by the International Astronomical Union, honours, women assistants paid 25 cents an hour, her work in arranging partnerships and equipment exchanges between astronomers, and a quotation from Cannon that she had concentrated on her work (self-report). University history-of-science biography; it contains a speculative remark linking her deafness to her work habits that is not used.

Library of Congress, New York World-Telegram and the Sun Newspaper Photograph Collection, item 96502154, 'Mrs. Annie Jump Cannon, head-and-shoulders portrait, left profile' (1922; credit 'Fotograms, N.Y. photo'). Holder record read for the portrait review only; the portrait is held.

Schlesinger Library, Radcliffe Institute, Harvard University, 'Portrait of Annie Jump Cannon' (1895-1897), Radcliffe College Archives PC 70-1-2, via Harvard LibraryCloud. Holder record read for the portrait review only (it states a reproduction restriction); the portrait is held.

discipline.rationale: [src_cannon_britannica, src_cannon_dsb, src_cannon_mactutor, src_cannon_scitimes | 1896-1941 | encyclopaedia, historical dictionary, university biography, reference entry] Britannica and the Dictionary record that she began classifying spectra in her first year at Harvard, that the Henry Draper Catalogue spectra were classified between 2 October 1911 and 30 September 1915 (Pickering's 1918 preface, quoted by MacTutor) and the volumes completed by 1924, that she then added about 47,000 classifications in the Extension and further zone catalogues, and that she retired officially in 1940 but carried on research until her death in 1941. Four independent reference works agree on a very large, steady output over decades; the numbers and the reasons for the pace rest on summaries.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_cannon_dsb, src_cannon_mactutor, src_cannon_scitimes | 1896-1915 | historical dictionary, university biography, reference entry] The Dictionary says her rate was more than three stars a minute and that the Draper classifications were made in the relatively brief interval from 1911 to 1915; MacTutor says her rate rose from 1,000 stars in three years to 200 an hour by 1913; Science and Its Times says 5,000 a month rising to about 300 an hour. The figures differ between sources but all describe a very high and increasing working pace on a repetitive classification task; it is a measure of throughput on one kind of work, so confidence is moderate.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_cannon_dsb, src_cannon_scitimes, src_cannon_mactutor | 1901-1924 | historical dictionary, reference entry, university biography] The Dictionary says she rarely failed to note the peculiarities in a spectrum and could duplicate her classifications later (a concrete consistency check), and Science and Its Times says she insisted that even the faintest stars be included and described each star's position, magnitudes and peculiarities, with every observation made by a single classifier; MacTutor adds that she was accurate without citing a check, and Payne-Gaposchkin's 'dispassionate and unbiased' is retrospective praise by a protegee. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70/0.52 because the accuracy evidence is mostly retrospective admiration and one unsourced remark.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait was found after one bounded retry. The Library of Congress photograph (item 96502154, dated 1922) is credited to 'Fotograms, N.Y. photo', not to the New York World-Telegram, and carries a 'publication may be restricted' advisory with no evidence of publication; the Schlesinger Library portrait (1895-1897) is marked by the Radcliffe Archives as not to be reproduced without written permission, contradicting its Flickr 'no known restrictions' label; the Harvard University Archives 1913 snapshot is a joint portrait with no creator, rights statement or identification of which woman is which; the Smithsonian Science Service prints have an unidentified photographer and no dated rights basis. Next step: locate a pre-1931 printed portrait with a stated photographer and publication date (for example a periodical or book plate on the Internet Archive), or obtain a written rights statement from the Radcliffe Archives or the Library of Congress.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (alt-dependent) (lead) / FAILED, PORTRAIT HELD. Every route failed on the holder's own record. (1) LEAD, Library of Congress NYWTS photograph 96502154 (read as JSON; the HTML page is Cloudflare-walled): date 1922, credit 'Fotograms, N.Y. photo', rights_advisory 'Publication may be restricted. For information see New York World-Telegram & ...', empty rights field. The lead's work-for-hire route (used for MLK, Malcolm X and Ali) does not apply: the World-Telegram did not exist in 1922 and the credit names a third-party agency, so the record materially weakens the claimed basis. An age-based route (published in the US before 1931) would need evidence of publication, which the record does not give, so it would be a speculative publication theory. The Commons file page for the same image is no better: its description is garbled and its source is a Britannica page. (2) ALTERNATIVE, Schlesinger Library portrait c.1895-1897 (Harvard LibraryCloud olvwork353777): the holder's accessCondition states that the image may not be reproduced without written permission from the Radcliffe Archives, which contradicts the Flickr/Commons 'no known copyright restrictions' label. (3) Harvard University Archives 1913 snapshot 'Annie J. Cannon [and] Henrietta S. Leavitt': joint full-length snapshot, no creator, no copyright statement ('no restrictions on access' only), and the record does not say which woman is which, so the sitter cannot be positively identified. (4) Smithsonian Institution Archives Science Service prints: unidentified photographer, no dated rights basis beyond the generic Flickr label. (5) Commons has no other photograph of her with a dated, credited, holder-documented source (the 1921 newspaper file is 172 x 273 pixels). NEXT STEP: find a pre-1931 print publication of a portrait with a stated photographer and publication date (a periodical or book plate on the Internet Archive), or ask the Radcliffe Archives or the Library of Congress for a written rights statement.
